candidate.title: A path-named program runs on the host when its basename is an allowed hunt audit form
candidate.description: The hunt guardrail judges the program by its basename. When the basename and arguments match an allowed audit form (date, npm audit, pip list, cargo audit, osv-scanner, pip-audit, and in this range gitleaks), the call is allowed and the rule that refuses a program named by a path inside the project is never run. A hunter steered by repository text can then run an executable file of the audited tree, or on Windows Git Bash a `#!` script it wrote into reviews/<id>/, under a name such as `./gitleaks` or `reviews/<id>/date`, directly on the host with the developer's credentials. This is outside the Docker sandbox, which AGENTS.md and the hunt contract make the only door to project code. A sibling control (`bash reviews/x.sh` is refused) shows the intent.
candidate.claimed_root_cause: In simple(), huntCheck is called with the basename-only prog and returns at `if (h && h.allow) { ...; return; }` before huntProgramWhy, which is the only place that refuses a path-named program inside the project.

trace.description: The program word, which may be a path such as ./gitleaks or reviews/<id>/date, becomes prog = progName(args[0].v).
progName keeps only the basename, lowercased, without .exe, so the directory part of the path is dropped.
gitleaks (and date at 798, osv-scanner at 874, the package managers) are judged by their arguments only and return allow() with no look at the path.
The refusal of a program that is a path inside the project exists only here, and it is reached only for programs huntCheck did not allow.
`if (h && h.allow) { ... return; }` ends the check, so the call passes and the shell starts the file at the given path.

evidence.description: huntCheck receives prog (the basename) and the argument values, never the original program word.
huntProgramWhy is called after the huntCheck return, so an allowed audit form never reaches it.
gitleaks was added to HUNT_AUDIT_TOOLS in this range (diff dev..GH-63-cloudflare-engine); the huntCheck-before-huntProgramWhy order itself is unchanged and already existed for the other tools.
The bash layer adds no executable-path rule for the hunt; it only runs the same analyzer (:1166).

blockers: No sandbox for this run, so the analyzer cannot be executed to observe the allow decision

Whether an executable named like an allowed tool exists in the audited tree (Linux), or whether MSYS runs a `#!` file written into reviews/<id>/ without an exec bit (Windows), is a deployment fact outside source

validation_plan.local: In a throwaway project with a hunt run record, feed hooks/qa-guardrail the PreToolUse event {tool_name: Bash, command: `./bin/gitleaks --version`} and then `reviews/<id>/date +%s` with a harmless shebang file there. Expect the analyzer to refuse a path-named program, as it does for `bash repo/script.sh`; an allow, or a run of the file, confirms the candidate.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner check: on the machine that runs hunts, create reviews/<id>/gitleaks as a one-line `#!/bin/sh` script that only prints a marker, and see whether a hunter session is allowed to run `reviews/<id>/gitleaks --version`.

checks.invariant: every program a hunt shell command starts is on the allow-list, and a program named by a path inside the project is refused (huntProgramWhy :1165-1177)
checks.result: The path-named-program refusal lives only in huntProgramWhy (:1169-1177). simple() takes progName(args[0].v), which is the basename (:72, :1725), calls huntCheck (:2128) and returns at :2130-2133 when huntCheck allows, before huntProgramWhy runs at :2139. Every program huntCheck allows is therefore started under whatever path the agent wrote: date, npm, pnpm, pip, dotnet, cargo, pip-audit, osv-scanner, and in this range gitleaks (:609, :889). No test covers a path-qualified audit tool (tests/qa-gatekeeper has no such case). Recorded as a candidate: hunt-guardrail/audit-form-skips-program-path-check.

checks.invariant: the plugin's own scripts the hunt may run with node (HUNT_OWN_SCRIPTS_RE, extended in this range with hunt-sandbox, hunt-verdict and the two validators) are the plugin's files, not the audited tree's
checks.result: huntProgramWhy (:1233-1256) requires the script to be the first word after node with no option, free of `..`, not stdin, matching the anchored regex on the real path, outside the report area, inside the real plugin root, and a regular file. The env gate (:2112-2116) refuses NODE_OPTIONS and the other loader variables before it. The arguments of these scripts are not judged by the guardrail, only by name for key material. The validators (validate-findings.cjs, validate-coverage-ledger.cjs) take one path, read it, and write nothing. The same-checkout case (plugin root equal to the audited project) trusts the audited tree by construction and is not a boundary here.

checks.invariant: a tool the hunt does not use, a tool that carries a URL, and a tracker or mail tool that writes are all denied in the hunt profile
checks.result: The hunt gate (:767-799) denies web fetch and search names, any non-reader tool with a URL, the write_stdin forms, and any tool not on hunt_write_re, hunt_shell_re or hunt_tools_re unless its MCP server is a tracker or mail word, so unknown MCP tools and other connectors (Drive, Calendar, Firecrawl, Canva) are denied. Tracker and mail tools pass as reads. The write-vs-read decision for them (:705-731) is a verb list in which `trash`, `mark`, `archive`, `request` and `apply` are missing, so Gmail trash_message, trash_thread, mark_message_spam and mark_thread_spam, and GitHub request_copilot_review, are classified as reads and pass (candidate hunt-guardrail/tracker-write-verb-denylist-misses-trash-mark).
